subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If P and Q are the sum of odd terms and the sum of even terms respectively in the expansion of (x + a)ⁿ, then prove that (i) P² − Q² = (x² − a²)ⁿ and (ii) 4PQ = (x + a)²ⁿ − (x − a)²ⁿ.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove both parts — what P and Q are, why (x + a)ⁿ is P + Q and (x − a)ⁿ is P − Q, and how multiplying gives (i) and squaring-and-subtracting gives (ii).
insider_note: P holds the odd TERMS, and the odd terms carry the EVEN powers of a. Sort by that and (x − a)ⁿ = P − Q comes in one line; sort by odd powers and both proofs break.

steps.label: Split (x + a)ⁿ into P + Q
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Odd terms are the 1st, 3rd, 5th… — they carry EVEN powers of a (a⁰, a², a⁴). Even terms carry odd powers of a.
steps.memory_tip: Odd TERMS carry EVEN powers of a — the 1st, 3rd, 5th hold a⁰, a², a⁴. P starts with ⁿC₀xⁿ.

recall.must_convey: That P collects the 1st, 3rd, 5th… terms (even powers of a) and Q the 2nd, 4th… terms (odd powers of a), so (x + a)ⁿ = P + Q.
accept: expand x plus a to the n, P is the odd terms with even powers of a, Q is the even terms with odd powers of a, so x plus a to the n is P plus Q
group the expansion into P the first third fifth terms and Q the second fourth sixth terms
x plus a to the n equals P plus Q
odd terms P, even terms Q, x plus a power n equals P plus Q
P has a to the even powers and Q has a to the odd powers

steps.why: The proof rests on one observation: P and Q differ in whether the power of a is even or odd, which is exactly what changing a to −a detects.
common_mistakes: Putting the odd POWERS of a into P — the odd TERMS carry even powers.
Forgetting that P starts with ⁿC₀xⁿ.

steps.label: Show (x − a)ⁿ = P − Q
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Replace a by −a: even powers of a are unchanged, odd powers change sign.
steps.memory_tip: Replace a by −a: even powers keep their sign, odd powers flip. So (x − a)ⁿ = P − Q.

odd powers of a change sign:

recall.must_convey: That replacing a by −a leaves P unchanged and changes the sign of Q, so (x − a)ⁿ = P − Q.

x minus a to the n equals P minus Q
the expansion of x minus a to the n is the same with alternating signs which is P minus Q

steps.why: (−a)ᵏ is aᵏ for even k and −aᵏ for odd k. That single fact converts the second expansion into P − Q with no new work.
common_mistakes: Re-expanding from scratch and grouping again.

steps.label: Prove (i) by multiplying
steps.margin_note: Fourth and fifth marks. (P + Q)(P − Q) = P² − Q² on one side, (x + a)ⁿ(x − a)ⁿ = ((x + a)(x − a))ⁿ on the other.
steps.memory_tip: P² − Q² = (P + Q)(P − Q) = (x + a)ⁿ(x − a)ⁿ = (x² − a²)ⁿ. The index stays n, not 2n.

recall.must_convey: That P² − Q² = (P + Q)(P − Q) = (x + a)ⁿ(x − a)ⁿ = (x² − a²)ⁿ.
accept: P squared minus Q squared is P plus Q into P minus Q which is x plus a to the n into x minus a to the n which is x squared minus a squared to the n
multiply one and two to get the difference of squares
P plus Q times P minus Q equals x plus a times x minus a all to the n
one and two multiply cheste P square minus Q square equals x square minus a square power n
difference of squares on both sides

steps.why: P² − Q² factorises as (P + Q)(P − Q), and both factors are already known as whole binomials.
common_mistakes: Trying to square P and Q term by term.

steps.label: Prove (ii) by squaring
steps.margin_note: Sixth and seventh marks. (P + Q)² − (P − Q)² = 4PQ is the identity; then substitute (1) and (2).
steps.memory_tip: (P + Q)² − (P − Q)² = 4PQ. Squaring (x + a)ⁿ doubles the index to 2n.

accept: four P Q is P plus Q squared minus P minus Q squared, which is x plus a to the two n minus x minus a to the two n

steps.why: (P + Q)² − (P − Q)² = 4PQ is a one-line algebra identity, and squaring (x + a)ⁿ doubles the index to 2n.
